In English, the name of one person, as t.why: Held as a usage pattern seen hundreds of thousands of times per name ('Harry is' alone 549,335 times in Dolma) and as the textbook rule that a verb agrees with its subject. Plural forms are not counted bare: 'Harry are' is dominated by coordinations ('Neville and Harry are').

sources.quote: one may say I am or he is, but not "I is" or "he am"

In a present-tense sentence, 'Zorvan', t.why: Zorvan is a name invented for the prompt: the sentence is not written anywhere, so only the rule plus the membership stated in the prompt gives the verb.

sources.note: Scattered uses of the name; none about height.
The rule, the other premise, as a usage pattern.

In a present-tense sentence, 'Melvara',.why: Melvara is a name invented for the prompt and never written with 'has'; the rule plus the membership gives the verb.

sources.note: AND query (max_clause_freq 500,000); the name is rare enough that the zero is not a sampling artefact.

In a present-tense sentence, 'Brannoc Ve.why: A full name invented for the prompt: no text has it, so the verb comes only from the rule.

In English spelling, a sentence begins w.why: True and taught everywhere: the first word of a sentence is capitalized.

sources.quote: In all modern European languages, the first word in a sentence is capitalized, as is the first word in any quoted sentence.

The past tense of the English verb 'run'.why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the edited rule: the past tense of 'run' is 'ran'.

notes: Template: TBox revision. The user's agreement edit ('Harry is good' to 'Harry are good'), made a rule about the class 'name of one person' so that it is a TBox edit; it covers the whole verb (is/are, has/have). Restricted to ordinary present-tense statements: the past subjunctive 'if Harry were here' and the mandative 'that Harry be' are correct today and kept out of every prompt. Coordinations ('Harry and Sally are') are not names of one person, and the group reading of a name (a band, 'Coldplay are') is not used (British collective agreement). Migrated to the new layout: the two indeterminate fixed-phrase queries ('Big Brother is watching you', 'Uncle Sam wants you') and their worlds were removed (TBox has determinate queries only); the three derived queries use names invented for the prompt (Zorvan, Melvara, Brannoc Velt), so the rule is the only route, and the third is an application (a mail-merge template) with an open question. Fill-in-the-blank wording was replaced by plain questions, and the propositional queries carry an example ('Harry are tall') so the abstract rule is easier to judge (the conjunction was missed by two models in the audit). Near unrelated: the pronoun 'she', a singular subject outside the class; an edit that spreads to every singular subject answers 'are' there. Agreement between a class of subjects and one verb form is a class inclusion with one filler: dl.
